title: Certify AI tools per use case, approve centrally, recertify on defined triggers
problem: Firm quality-management processes were built for transparent, deterministic tools, so it is hard to decide how much testing AI tools need before deployment and how to monitor them afterwards.
approach: UK regulator FRC says each tool is certified within a use case, testing outputs on default, edge and known-weakness cases.
Recertification may be triggered by material change, a different use case, performance issues, changed standards or elapsed time.
Deloitte UK's Technology Controls Board, set up in April 2026, reviews tools before pilot and deployment; no measure is given (self-reported).
Tool owner, methodology and business sign off certification; quality leadership decides whether to recertify after a trigger event.

title: Risk-tiered policy: approved AI tools, barred uses, triage and a prompt library
problem: Staff will use general AI tools unless told which are allowed; most of the six largest UK firms certified every tool identically, regardless of risk.
approach: Firms list permitted tools and uses, bar some uses and scale validation to risk, with a central triage step for new proposals.
PwC US gave staff AI training and LLM access for pre-approved work such as administrative tasks before launching audit-specific AI.
Deloitte UK describes risk thresholding, triage and a clearing house for GenAI use cases; no result is published (self-reported).
A clearing house decides the tier before build or purchase; the methodology owner approves each permitted use case and prompt set.
who: PwC US, Deloitte UK, FRC, PCAOB staff

title: Inventory of approved AI tools, with controls against unapproved or outdated use
problem: AI tools multiply faster than firms approve them and staff can reach public chatbots; the FRC found firms generally did not monitor that teams used only authorised, current tools.
approach: Firms keep inventories of current certified tools and versions, relying on preventive controls such as approved repositories and blocking unauthorised installs.
Most of the six largest UK firms kept such inventories; usage monitoring mainly counted teams using tools, typically for licensing (independent).
More than a third of surveyed tax and audit professionals admit using unauthorised AI tools (vendor-published).
A named function approves exceptions, unapproved tools found in use are escalated, and engagement reviews check for incorrect use.

title: Evaluation sets and parallel running before full rollout of an AI tool
problem: No public benchmark or firm result says how often an audit AI tool's output is wrong in live use, and tolerance for deficient output remains a professional judgement.
approach: Firms build representative test sets and score tool output against them before release and after model changes.
IFIAR lists benchmarking against traditional methods and false-positive and false-negative rates versus a manual sample as emerging practice.
FRC: tools may go to a few teams before full certification, and teams often perform the alternative procedures in parallel.
No parallel-run results are published; methodology specialists agree pass criteria and the quality team decides when a pilot ends.

title: Embed methodology in AI tool design and validate the assurance it provides
problem: Methodology can permit approaches that fail auditing standards even if a tool works; IFIAR's most frequent findings were misreading tool results and thin outlier testing.
approach: Methodology teams join tool development and approve how output is used as evidence; certification validates methodology against auditing standards.
FRC example: assurance from the AI procedure rests on confidence in its risk indicators and sampling, which sets remaining substantive testing.
Most of the six largest UK firms capture methodology-team sign-off in certification documents (independent).
IFIAR: 31% of members (2024) and 29% (2023) reported findings that a tool was not used as intended (independent).

title: Due diligence and contracts for third-party AI tools, scaled for smaller firms
problem: Firms usually get the foundation model from a third party and often cannot evaluate its training data or logic, and smaller firms lack specialists to assess it.
approach: All six largest UK firms weighed vendor controls, data security and confidentiality when choosing tools (FRC finding); no outcome is published.
Where information is unavailable, the FRC says firms may rely on independent assurance and test more themselves.
NFRA staff call for contract terms on data protection, audit rights and continuity; CPAB suggests a SOC 2 report on IT controls.
Procurement, security and methodology approve the vendor, and the firm re-approves the tool when the vendor changes the model.

title: Monitor AI tool use and audit-quality impact with metrics and dashboards
problem: Firms count tool usage, mostly for licensing, but do not quantify the effect on audit quality, and it is sometimes unclear who monitors globally developed tools.
approach: IFIAR examples: thematic reviews with metrics such as false-positive and false-negative rates against a manual sample, plus usage dashboards.
AFM found engagement-level usage was estimated for 74% of auditing tools, actual data for 20%, unclear for 6% (independent).
FRC: none of the six largest UK firms formally quantified audit-quality impact; one reported usage against targets for certain key tools (independent).
Quality leaders review impact metrics and decide to restrict, retrain or recertify a tool.

title: Board-level AI oversight in the quality plan, with escalation channels
problem: Using AI tools reaches beyond technology resources into governance, ethics and engagement performance, and unexpected AI failures may not reach the tool owner or quality function.
approach: Deloitte UK's independent Audit Governance Board reviewed its quality plan, now covering AI, with a human in the loop central (self-reported).
Deloitte UK's Chief AI Officer is responsible for embedding responsible AI governance across client services and internal operations.
IFIAR suggests formal escalation paths for unexpected outputs, user feedback, AI oversight committees and whistleblowing procedures covering AI use.
A committee or tool owner decides whether to pause, restrict or re-approve a tool after an incident; no outcome is published.

title: Get the firm's own AI management system certified to ISO/IEC 42001
problem: Firms need external reference points for governing their own AI use; SEC staff said there is no single authority or framework for AI governance, speaking of preparers, not audit firms.
approach: KPMG announced in November 2025 that it achieved ISO 42001 certification of its internal AI management systems (self-reported).
KPMG called it a necessary precursor to AI assurance services and said it is the first Big Four firm to achieve it.
The announcement does not say which KPMG entity was certified, and no quality measurement is published.

title: Role-based AI training tied to tool access, with in-workflow micro-training
problem: Reviewers who cannot judge when AI output is wrong cannot review it; untrained staff was the top-ranked blocker to audit transformation in a survey of 54 US CPA firms.
approach: Training is tailored by user group; the FRC says it should cover reviewing tool output, automation bias (over-trusting machines) and known weaknesses.
PwC made GenAI training mandatory before ChatPwC access and KPMG trained all auditors in prompt engineering (2024 reports, per an academic reading).
Deloitte announced on 24 June 2026 a 'tutor mode' in Omnia giving on-demand micro-training within the work (self-reported).
Tool access is conditional on completed training; no measure of training's effect on review quality is published.

title: Connected engagement resourcing: staffing, budgets and leader review in one tool
problem: The quality standard ISQM 1 requires firms to assign people with the competence and capacity for each engagement; RSM describes replacing manual staffing and budgeting processes.
approach: RSM's Luca Resourcing is a connected tool for initial staffing requests, budget planning and engagement-leader review, giving teams visibility of planning.
RSM lists it among its AI-related investments but does not say what AI does inside it.
The engagement leader reviews and approves the staffing plan and budget; no outcome is published (self-reported).
IRBA cites AI analysis of staff profiles and experience for resource optimisation as an example in audit planning.

title: Firm-approved guidance assistant for audit research, grounded in the firm's own manuals
problem: Auditors spend time finding and applying the firm's own assurance manuals and guides and may apply them inconsistently, while generic chatbots can produce hallucinations, omissions and distortions.
approach: RSM US launched Ask Luca on 8 January 2026, drawing on its assurance manuals and guides for 4,000+ assurance professionals (self-reported).
Deloitte UK launched a Research Assistant chatbot for audit research; PCAOB staff heard some firms built tools to research internal guidance.
No time, accuracy or consistency measure is published.
The auditor checks the source guidance and applies own judgement; complex or novel questions still go to technical consultation.
who: RSM US, Deloitte UK, PCAOB staff

title: Engage regulators early on new AI tools and keep inspection-ready tool files
problem: Standards do not yet address AI directly, yet regulators say they will inspect AI use and are still working out whether new standards or documentation rules are needed.
approach: PCAOB inspectors meet firms, generally larger ones, to understand their AI use; many invited inspectors to demonstrations while piloting.
FRC's Audit Tech & AI Sandbox opened 4 June 2026: about three expert meetings for selected UK firms, with no endorsement.
A central file per tool holds its purpose, development, certification and training, drawing on the FRC's split of documentation.
Quality leadership decides what to bring to regulators and when; sandbox participants are not named and no outcome is published.

title: Idea: use AI in the firm's own quality monitoring and root-cause analysis
problem: Idea only, no deployment: IFIAR counted 21 findings in 2025 (6 in 2024) for firms failing to identify audit performance issues in internal inspections.
approach: The SEC's chief accountant said the SEC asks auditors how they use AI to monitor their system of quality control.
NFRA's staff paper calls for root-cause analysis of technology-related findings to feed the annual evaluation of the quality system.
No firm example was found; the FRC noted tool use may appear in root-cause analysis without saying AI does the analysis.
Quality leadership would decide which root causes are real; remediation owners would sign off actions.

title: Idea: independent validation or assurance of audit firms' own AI tools
problem: Idea only, not a deployment: smaller firms without in-house expertise may want someone to confirm a tool works as intended; the market is fragmented and not regulated traditionally.
approach: Deloitte's Martin Brown said third-party providers should be doing testing and evaluation for the use case (ICAEW podcast).
Grant Thornton UK's Jon Morris said smaller firms would probably favour a provider partnered with a large firm; early days.
No outcome is published; the firm would decide what weight to give a third-party validation when approving a tool.

title: Firm-wide audit programmes on an AI platform, updated centrally after inspection findings
problem: Sanville & Company, a 20-person firm on a legacy platform, found sample-heavy testing created bottlenecks at partner and quality review as QC 1000 approached.
approach: Sanville built its audit programmes in Fieldguide, referencing PCAOB standards in each step, and sent templates to every engagement at once.
Agentic testing handled sample-heavy tracing of incoming client support.
After a PCAOB exam flagged an issue, the partner updated the programme and pushed it to every open engagement next morning.
First PCAOB inspection fully on the platform had zero comment forms; overhaul took under a year versus 18-24 months expected (vendor-published).

title: Idea: plan AI use at the outset and review it before sign-off
problem: Idea only, no deployment: the engagement partner is responsible for direction, supervision and review, but tool outputs that are hard to explain or invite over-reliance complicate this.
approach: IFIAR asks engagement leaders to set expectations at the outset for how technology will be used, including planned uses of AI.
IFIAR also asks senior team members to reflect at the end on technology use in the file and whether scepticism was maintained.
The AICPA practice aid recommends planning intended AI use; partners must understand the tools and ensure the firm approved them.
The engagement leader would approve the planned AI uses; IRBA places responsibility for appropriate use on the engagement partner.

title: Human control points in AI-agent audit workflows, with escalation and approval
problem: Agents run multi-step procedures, so there is no single output to review; without defined review points errors compound and reviewers either redo everything or accept plausible output.
approach: The FRC separates final-output review from oversight at control points (intermediate results, planned actions), and lets the tool escalate when uncertain.
IFIAR asks firms to assign specific personnel to decision checkpoints; IAASB roundtable participants called human-in-the-loop oversight non-negotiable.
Deloitte UK says teams critically assess, corroborate and approve agent results before use; KPMG says agents work 'in concert with human review'.
Deloitte and KPMG describe this as design intent and report no review results or control-point catches (self-reported).

title: Review mechanics for AI output: citations, source tie-back and confirmation gates
problem: A confident, well-formatted AI output can pass review with less challenge than a junior's work, and fluent output without sources cannot be checked efficiently.
approach: FRC worked examples have the tool cite stable document identifiers for every extract, which supports review and reduces fabrication.
AFM saw good practice where each workflow step completes only once the auditor confirms the output was reviewed and supported by evidence.
Fieldguide says each agent run keeps a Trace of inputs, outputs and reasoning (vendor-published); PwC and RSM describe similar evidence trails.
No measured detection or override rate is published; reviewers confirm each AI-assisted step and check cited sources.

title: Idea: reviewers form an independent view before reading the AI's answer
problem: Idea only, no deployment: in an experiment, auditors relying on automated tools were less sceptical than when relying on a team member's work.
approach: The FRC says review may mean forming an independent view to compare, such as reading source material to confirm a GenAI summary.
In the Peters experiment a counter-arguing mindset intervention alleviated the loss of scepticism; it concerned automated tools, not GenAI (independent).
The AFM saw auditors make their own fraud-risk assessment first, then use a GenAI tool to challenge it.
Reviewer records an independent view before opening AI output; a supervisor spot-checks the quality of challenge.

title: AI checks of audit files for omissions and inconsistencies before reviewer sign-off
problem: Reviewers spend time on completeness and consistency checks that cost attention needed for judgemental areas, and review is a bottleneck.
approach: Deloitte UK: GenAI tool Smart Review fully deployed in the year to 31 May 2025; all FTSE audits have access (self-reported).
KPMG says agents in KPMG Clara can assist teams by reviewing engagement documentation.
PIA Group's Group CIO describes hundreds, in some cases more than 1,000, AI checks per file (interview claim, not measured).
Reviewers resolve every AI-raised exception and still review judgemental areas; neither firm describes how reviewers use the output.

title: Idea: cross-check AI output with a second model or rules-based tool
problem: Idea only, no deployment: generative tools are probabilistic, the same prompt can give different outputs, and human reviewers cannot catch every deficiency in high-volume AI output.
approach: FRC guidance lists one AI model reviewing another's work, several models attempting a task, and rules-based checks such as schema checking.
As reported, the AICPA practice aid says one AI tool may check another, but the auditor's review responsibility is not reduced.
Grant Thornton UK's Jon Morris put AI reviewing AI 'a few years down the line'; no result is published.
The process escalates to a human when components disagree or the checker is unsure.

title: Record AI use centrally per tool and on each engagement file
problem: Inspectors and reviewers cannot challenge AI-assisted work if the file does not show where AI was used and how the team responded; the AFM found this not always clear.
approach: FRC guidance keeps a tool's purpose, development, certification and training centrally; the engagement file holds version, prompts and how outputs informed conclusions.
IFIAR asks firms to identify GenAI use in critical audit areas and to explain how auditor judgement was applied to outputs.
FRC: firms with engagement-specific tool processes all required templates on the audit file, though some wording made completion look optional (independent).
A named reviewer records reasons for each AI-assisted procedure; none of four UK Big Four 2024 reports stated override frequency (independent).

title: Disclose AI use to clients and audit committees via engagement-letter terms
problem: Clients worry about where their data goes and whether it trains models; a Grant Thornton UK director said some clients were nervous and a few would not sign up.
approach: Grant Thornton UK uses clear engagement-letter terms on AI use and in some cases ring-fences work from model training.
Deloitte's Martin Brown said very few clients had asked the firm not to use GenAI, and that transparency and education matter.
A Foley article suggests audit committees ask what the auditor does with AI, under what controls, and how AI-assisted judgements are documented.
The engagement leader agrees AI-use terms with the client and audit committee; no measure is published (self-reported).

title: Redesign supervision and early-career development as juniors review AI output
problem: If tools do the first-pass work juniors used to do, juniors lose the practice that built judgement while being asked to review tool output.
approach: PwC's AI assurance leader said in August 2025 that new hires would act like managers within three years by overseeing AI.
PwC says assurance training is moving back to basics, with earlier time on critical thinking, negotiation and professional scepticism.
IFIAR asks firms to prioritise supervision training; the Thomson Reuters Institute says juniors still need structured development and supervision.
No outcome is published; baseline: 31 IFIAR findings on supervision and review policies in 2025, up from 10 in 2024 (independent).
who: PwC, IFIAR, Thomson Reuters Institute, CPAB
